This is because EVs are considered to be flexible over a 3-day period, and on the peak day prices are consistently high enough to move all charging load into the neighboring days. Cooling daytime load increases are significant throughout the morning and early afternoon, adding 3-6 GW of load in all hours except for the 11am-12pm hour, when significant shed occurs. This enables a cooling load reduction of over 2 GW throughout the evening, with a cooling load reduction of 5.9 GW in the peak hour. Combined with all other end uses, the system net load is reduced 8.75 GW in the peak hour. The system net load impacts are further illustrated in Figure 15, which shows the impact of highly coordinated load response on the mid-day system net load shape. On average, the “take” period for end use loads is highly concentrated between 10am and 2pm, causing a dip in the system net load at 9am before jumping back up, and a deeper “belly” of the duck moved to later in the day, when prices start to rise, and customers are incentivized to start shedding load. This “belly” is higher than the baseline, which is good for supporting renewables integration and reducing curtailment, but the double ramp periods may pose operational challenges for generators that are not meant to ramp up and down multiple times throughout the day (e.g. combined cycle gas turbines (Espinoza et al. 2014)). On the (baseline) peak net load day, the net load curve is essentially flattened from midnight to 3pm, oscillating between 25-30 GW with a somewhat erratic nature due to the highly coordinated response of the end use loads (particularly the steep cooling shed at 11am). The net load then rises to an evening plateau at approximately 43 GW, which as discussed, is 8 GW lower than the baseline peak. 29 Figure 14.
